note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Wasp sting while gardening ~15 minutes prior; developing breathing difficulties since then.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset ~15 minutes ago with shallow breathing and chest tightness; lip tingling sensation; blotching rash on body.
  - Denies throat swelling; no hoarseness or dysphagia reported.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Lip tingling without notable lip/face swelling; no throat swelling or stridor described.
- Past medical history and treatments:
  - History notable for eczema.
  - Penicillin allergy.
  - No prior similar episodes reported.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergic to penicillin.
  - At home: antihistamines available (used previously for flying/aerosinusitis); dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Social context:
  - Wife present; patient able to be transported to hospital; doctor advised ambulance.

Objective:
- Observable findings:
  - Lip tingling reported; no visible lip/face swelling described.
  - Body blotching rash observed.
- Airway/breathing:
  - Breathing described as shallow with chest tightness; no stridor noted.
- Mental status:
  - Not described.
- Vitals/examination:
  - Not recorded.
- Support person:
  - Wife accompanying; present during encounter.

Assessment:
- Suspected anaphylactic reaction to wasp sting given rapid onset after sting, respiratory symptoms (shallow breathing, chest tightness), lip/skin symptoms (lip tingling, blotching rash), and potential for rapid progression.
- No throat swelling reported at this time; no prior similar episodes.

Plan:
- Immediate actions:
  - Advise ambulance to be called; patient to go to emergency department.
  - While awaiting ambulance, administer antihistamine (noted as available at home) to patient; exact dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Instructions to patient/caregiver:
  - Have wife call emergency services immediately; remain with patient; ambulance transport arranged for rapid assessment.
  - Use antihistamine now as advised while awaiting EMS.
  - Seek urgent care in ED for potential anaphylaxis; monitor for progression (breathing difficulty, throat swelling, wheeze, dizziness, faintness).
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  - Worsening breathing, throat swelling, new wheeze, chest tightness, lip/face swelling, or dizziness.
- Follow-up:
  - Not specified in transcript; implied evaluation in ED and allergy/ENT follow-up as appropriate.

Document quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Exact allergy list beyond penicillin, prior anaphylaxis management plan, auto-injector availability, detailed current medications with doses, prior ED visits.
  - Vital signs and formal ENT exam findings.
- Internal conflicts:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality:
  - Clear presentation of an acute allergic reaction scenario with escalating support needs; some details (dose/routes) not documented.
